output.title: Maintenance windows are a workflow choice, not a calendar slot
output.body:
For a 1–10-person business, rethinking maintenance windows is really a workflow decision: do you bundle changes into planned downtime, spread them through rolling updates, or use a hybrid? The question is not which one sounds modern. It is which one costs you less in practice: planned customer-visible outage or unplanned breakdowns.

The useful diagnostic is simple: do you already have a repeatable maintenance routine? If you have a standard pre-maintenance message, a checklist, a rollback step, and a log of what changed, that is a sign the process may be worth tightening. In that case, automation can help with sequencing, reminders, and record-keeping. It should not make the go/no-go call for you. Human approval still belongs at the point where service might be interrupted or risk increases.

If the work is mostly email, notes, and tool-jumping, start by mapping the handoffs before trying to automate anything. Otherwise you end up with a tidy machine around a messy habit. Clever, but not useful.

Bareni treats this as a bounded workflow question, not a promise that AI belongs everywhere. A free 30-minute diagnostic can identify the one recurring workflow, check whether AI fits, and—if it does—define a narrow pilot boundary with the owner still making the final call. Some maintenance setups are a fit for that kind of review; others are better left manual. The point is to see the boundary clearly before you invest time on the wrong side of it.
